meta.title: Who really said "Adversity introduces a man to himself"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Einstein. The line first appears in print in 1945, in a US railway union magazine, credited to 'ANONYMOUS' — and it was still being called anonymous in the New York Times in 1970. The 1922 Nobel ceremony story fails twice: Einstein wasn't there.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Adversity introduces a man to himself'?
meta.ogDescription: Anonymous from the day it was printed — 1945, credited 'ANONYMOUS'. The popular story that Einstein said it at the 1922 Nobel ceremony collapses on a simple fact: he didn't attend.

answer.label: Nobody famous — printed as ‘Anonymous’ from the start
answer.sourceLine: There is no Einstein source — no letter, no interview, no speech, nothing in the archives or in Alice Calaprice’s collections. The earliest printing anyone has located is 1945, in a US railway union magazine, where it is credited to ‘ANONYMOUS’. It was still being introduced as an anonymous saying in the New York Times twenty-five years later. The story that Einstein said it at the 1922 Nobel ceremony fails on a fact anyone can check: he was not at that ceremony.

source.excerpt: Adversity introduces a man to himself. — ANONYMOUS
trail: The quotation researcher Barry Popik ran the phrase through digitised American print. The earliest exact instance is 1945, in The Conductor and Brakeman — the magazine of a US railway union, volumes 62–63, page 168 — where it is printed as a filler line with the credit ‘ANONYMOUS’ already attached the citations ↗.

It moves into newspapers on 1 January 1946, in Josephine Lowman’s syndicated column ‘Why Grow Old?’ in the Greensboro Record — again as ‘Anonymous.’ That is the tell. A saying that arrives already labelled anonymous, in a filler slot, is a proverb doing what proverbs do; it is not a misplaced quotation from a famous man.

There are older cousins but no parent. William Beloe’s The Sexagenarian (1818) has ‘a literary life, like adversity, introduces a man to strange and opposite acquaintance’; an Alabama newspaper in 1895 has ‘practical education introduces a man to himself.’ And as late as 19 April 1970, the New York Times was still writing ‘it has been said that adversity introduces a man to himself’ — the formula you use when there is nobody to name.
source.excerptNote: The earliest located printing, with the credit as it appeared. Note that the anonymity is not something later researchers imposed — it is on the line the first time it shows up in print.

source.rightsNote: Free to reproduce. The saying is anonymous, first printed in 1945 in a US periodical, and no author or estate has ever claimed it — there is nobody to hold a copyright in six words nobody wrote. Since it is not Einstein’s, the tangle around Einstein’s own texts (public domain in the UK and EU since 1 January 2026, unresolved in the US, actively asserted by the Hebrew University of Jerusalem) does not apply here at all. Just do not attach his name. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Albert Einstein
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Einstein
author.bio: Albert Einstein (1879–1955) is the most misquoted person in modern history, and the reason is structural: he is the default author for any sentence that sounds wise and has no owner. This one is a textbook case — an anonymous American proverb from the 1940s that drifted onto his name decades later, helped along by his own biography of exile and refusal. Alice Calaprice’s collections exist precisely to sort the real Einstein from this traffic, and they catalogue the false attributions as carefully as the genuine lines. This sentence appears in neither list.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This one comes with a story attached, which is unusual and makes it easy to test. The story is that Einstein said it at his Nobel ceremony in 1922. It fails in two separate places, either of which would be enough.

items.why: No letter, interview, speech or manuscript. Nothing in the Einstein Archives, nothing in Calaprice’s collections — which catalogue the famous fakes as well as the genuine lines, so absence there is meaningful. The credit appears on quote aggregators with no citation at all.

items.who: Einstein was not at that ceremony
items.why: Einstein was awarded the 1921 physics prize in November 1922 and was travelling in Asia when it was presented in Stockholm on 10 December 1922; the German ambassador accepted on his behalf. He gave his Nobel lecture later, in Gothenburg in July 1923, and it was about relativity. The occasion the story requires did not exist.

The phrase has no located instance before 1945. If Einstein had said it in front of an audience in 1922, it would not take a railway union magazine twenty-three years to print it — and it would not have arrived credited to ‘ANONYMOUS’ when it did the citations ↗.

Mencken’s name circulates too, on the strength of his being a quotation-dictionary compiler. No edition or page has been produced that credits him as author, and we found none. Every serious trace ends at the same place: anonymous.

misattribution.truthLine: An anonymous American saying, first located in print in 1945 and labelled ‘ANONYMOUS’ on that first appearance. Einstein has no documented connection to it, and the 1922 Nobel ceremony he is supposed to have said it at is one he did not attend the trail ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is a genuinely good line, which is the awkward part. Six words, one idea, and a claim that survives contact with experience: you find out what you are made of only when something goes wrong, and the introduction is usually unflattering.

It also arrived at exactly the right moment. 1945 in America is a country coming out of depression and war with a lot of people who had just met themselves under pressure. A proverb like that does not need an author; it needs a filler slot in a union magazine, which is precisely what it got.
detailsBody: 1818: William Beloe, The Sexagenarian — ‘a literary life, like adversity, introduces a man to strange and opposite acquaintance.’ The shape, not the sentence.
23 October 1895: the Troy (Alabama) Messenger — ‘practical education introduces a man to himself, and then to humanity.’
1945: The Conductor and Brakeman, p. 168 — the exact wording, credited ‘ANONYMOUS’.
1 January 1946: Josephine Lowman’s ‘Why Grow Old?’ column in the Greensboro Record — again ‘Anonymous’.
19 April 1970: the New York Times — ‘it has been said that adversity introduces a man to himself.’ Still nobody to name.
Sometime after that, on the internet, it became Einstein’s. Nobody has documented when, and we are not going to invent a date.
context.pull: It arrived in print already credited to 'ANONYMOUS'. That is not a lost attribution — that is the attribution.
